extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and publishers seeking Chicago-style guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for capitalization, italicization, punctuation, and treatment of names, scientific terms, trademarks, software/devices, and titles of works according to The Chicago Manual of Style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of military organizations and units
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of military organizations, services, and units are capitalized (e.g., Royal Air Force; United States Marine Corps; Thirty-Third Infantry Division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common full names and accepted short forms (RAF, Coast Guard). Provide branch qualifiers when appropriate (Royal Canadian Navy (a branch of the Canadian Forces)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of wars and revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of most major wars and revolutions are capitalized; generic terms are usually lowercased when used alone; more recent, unresolved conflicts can usually be lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: World War II; the Civil War (American Civil War); but the South Sudanese civil war; the Ukrainian unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of battles and campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of major battles and campaigns that have entered the general lexicon are capitalized; in generic descriptions only proper names are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Battle of Britain; Battle of Bunker Hill; third battle of Ypres (note lowercase 'third' in running form). For unfamiliar names, consult an encyclopedia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of medals and awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific names of medals and awards are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Medal of Honor; Victoria Cross; Distinguished Flying Cross. For civil awards, consult relevant section (8.83).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of ships and vessels: italics and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of specific ships and other vessels are both capitalized and italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write the word ship or vessel when an abbreviation such as USS or HMS precedes the name; the abbreviation itself is not italicized. Use hull numbers where necessary to avoid confusion (e.g., USS Enterprise (CVN-65)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pronouns for vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pronoun is used to refer to a vessel, the neuter it or its is preferred instead of she or her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also cross-references (5.43, 8.77).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of other vehicle and program names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of makes/classes of aircraft, automobile models, trains, and space programs are capitalized but not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Acela Express; Boeing 787 Dreamliner; Project Apollo; Subaru Forester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicization and capitalization of scientific (binomial) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin names of species are italicized. Each binomial contains a genus name (capitalized) and a species name (specific epithet, lowercased).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smilodon; Rosa caroliniana; Styrax californica. Do not italicize phyla, orders, and higher ranks (see 8.126).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation of genus name after first use
rubrics_metrics.description: After the first use the genus name may be abbreviated to a single capital letter (e.g., C. coum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two or more species of the same genus are listed together, the abbreviation may be doubled to indicate the plural, though repeating the abbreviation for each species is more common. Avoid abbreviations when different genera beginning with the same letter appear in the same context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicization of subspecies and varieties; horticultural abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: A subspecific zoological name or epithet follows the binomial and is italicized; horticultural abbreviations (subsp., var., f.) are not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Noctilio labialis labialis (or Noctilio l. labialis); Buxus microphylla var. japonica; Hydrangea anomala subsp. petiolaris.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations 'sp.' and 'spp.' for unspecified taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: The abbreviations 'sp.' and 'var.' indicate that a species or variety is unknown or unspecified; 'spp.' refers to a group of species. These abbreviations are not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rhododendron spp.; Viola sp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic author names formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the person who proposed a specific epithet is sometimes added, often abbreviated, and never italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parentheses around an author indicate the species was originally described in a different genus (zoological usage). In botanical usage, the person who referred it to a new genus is added after the parentheses. Examples provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for plant hybrids
rubrics_metrics.description: The crossing of two species is indicated by a multiplication sign (×) between the two species names, with space on each side; some hybrid names use the multiplication sign immediately before the specific epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Magnolia denudata x M. liliiflora (crossing of species); Magnolia × soulangeana (hybrid name). Use the multiplication sign (not the letter x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of higher taxonomic divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions higher than genus—phylum, class, order, and family—are capitalized but not italicized. Terms like 'order' or 'family' (the common nouns) are not capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chordata (phylum); Monotremata (order); Hominidae (family); Felinae (subfamily).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercasing English derivatives of taxonomic names
rubrics_metrics.description: English words derived from the taxonomic system are lowercased and treated as ordinary English words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: carnivores (from Carnivora); hominids (from Hominidae); feline(s) (from Felinae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of vernacular common names for plants and animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago recommends capitalizing only proper nouns and adjectives in common names of plants and animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dutchman’s-breeches; Cooper’s hawk; Rocky Mountain sheep. For authoritative spelling and capitalization consult a dictionary or nomenclature guides (ICN, ICZN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of domestic breeds and horticultural categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult dictionaries or authoritative guides (ICZN, ICN) for proper spelling and capitalization of breeds and broad horticultural categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: German shorthaired pointer; Rhode Island Red; Maine coon (or coon cat). Note usage differences such as 'Thoroughbred horse' but 'purebred dog'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of horticultural cultivar names
rubrics_metrics.description: Horticultural cultivars often have registered or fanciful names that must be respected and may be enclosed in single quotation marks; any following punctuation is placed after the closing quotation mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the English name follows the Latin name, no intervening punctuation. Example: Agastache 'Apricot Sunrise'; Phygelius 'Salmon Leap'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic rules for gene and protein nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of genes or gene symbols are usually italicized; human gene symbols are in full capitals, other organisms vary (e.g., mouse genes often initial capital). Symbols for proteins (gene products) are set in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: BRCA1 (human gene); Cmv1 (mouse gene); GIF (gene symbol) vs GIF (gastric intrinsic factor). Consult HGNC and organism-specific databases for authoritative symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of enzyme names
rubrics_metrics.description: Enzyme names consist of a string of italic and roman characters: the first three letters (representing the organism name) are italicized; the roman numeral that follows is the series number; strain letters or arabic numerals may intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aval BamHI ClaI EcoRI HindIII Sau3AI. This illustrates the mixed italic/roman form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal vs generic geological-term capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal geological terms are capitalized in both noun and adjective forms; terms used generically are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Archean (eon) vs an eon; the Mesoproterozoic (era) vs the Mesoproterozoic era (formal). Modifiers early/middle/late: capitalized when formal, lowercased when informal (Early Archean but early Middle Cambrian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of formal stratigraphic names
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal stratigraphic names are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Morrison Formation; Niobrara Member; Fleur de Lys Supergroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of astronomical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of galaxies, constellations, stars, planets, and similar celestial bodies are capitalized. 'Earth' may be capitalized when used as the proper name of our planet, especially in contexts with other planets; 'sun' and 'moon' are usually lowercased in nontechnical contexts and always lowercased in the plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Milky Way; Alpha Centauri; Saturn; the astronauts have returned successfully to Earth; some publications in astronomy may capitalize sun and moon as proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog names for celestial objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Celestial objects listed in well-known catalogs are designated by the catalog name (often abbreviated) and a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NGC 6165; L1251; Bond 619.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive astronomical terms not capitalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely descriptive terms applied to celestial objects or phenomena are not capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aurora borealis; interstellar dust; the rings of Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of medical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of diseases, syndromes, diagnostic procedures, anatomical parts, and the like are lowercased, except for proper names forming part of the term; acronyms and initialisms are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or AIDS; Alzheimer disease; computed tomography or CT; Down syndrome. Possessive forms (Alzheimer’s, Down’s) may be preferred in general contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of names of infectious organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of infectious organisms are treated like other specific names (italicization rules apply); common forms of such names and names of conditions based on them are neither italicized nor capitalized, except for proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Microorganisms of the genus Streptococcus; the Ebola virus (named from the Ebola River).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of drug names and brands
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic names of drugs should be used where possible and are lowercased; brand names must be capitalized and are often given in parentheses after the first use of the generic name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: interferon beta-1a (Avonex). Consult AMA Manual of Style and USP Dictionary for guidance on brand and trade names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercasing names of laws and theories; chemical names and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of laws, theories, and the like are lowercased except for proper names attached to them; chemical element and compound names are lowercased when written out, but symbols are capitalized and set without periods; mass numbers are formatted differently in formal vs general contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the big bang theory; Boyle’s law; ozone (O3); carbon-14 (informal) vs 14C (formal); U-238 (informal) vs 238U (formal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling and usage of radiation terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms for electromagnetic radiations may be spelled in shorthand (B-ray, y-ray, x-ray) or in full (beta ray, gamma ray, x-ray), with usage depending on context; the verb 'to x-ray' is acceptable in general contexts but not normally in scholarly medical literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use radiograph or 'obtain an x-ray image' in scholarly medical writing instead of the verb to x-ray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric unit spellings and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago shows a preference for traditional American spellings (meter, liter) though European spellings are widely used; follow SI abbreviations per guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See SI abbreviations (10.51-59) for abbreviations and further rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of trademarks and brand names
rubrics_metrics.description: Brand names that are trademarks should be capitalized if used; it is better to use a generic term when available. The symbols ® and ™ should be omitted wherever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trademark symbol must be used it should appear before any final punctuation. Examples: Kleenex (facial tissue), Coca-Cola; prefer 'cola' or 'facial tissue' as generic alternatives when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of brand names with internal capitalization or all-lowercase styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Brand names with internal capital letters (intercaps/midcaps) or an initial lowercase followed by a capital need not be capitalized at the beginning of a sentence; names written entirely in lowercase should receive an initial capital at the beginning of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: iTunes is both an app and a media service; Mini is capitalized even midsentence; do capitalize fully lowercase brand names at sentence start to signal a proper noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting names of software, apps, operating systems, and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: References to specific applications, operating systems, and devices are set in roman type without quotation marks; capitalization usually reflects the usage displayed by the software or device itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the program's help menu or user guide for preferred styling. Examples: Microsoft Word; the Maps app for iOS 10; Firefox; the Kindle app. Generic references (a browser, a word processor) are ordinary text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview: treatment of titles in text and notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles mentioned or cited in text or notes are usually capitalized headline-style; for titles that deviate on covers or title pages, editorial discretion may apply; for non-English titles see separate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to titles of books, journals, newspapers, websites, shorter works, parts/chapters, unpublished works, plays, films, broadcasts, musical works, art works, etc. See chapters 14 and 15 for bibliographic citation specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-style capitalization for titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentence-style capitalization, only the first word in a title, the first word in a subtitle, and any proper names are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence style is commonly used in library catalogs and some reference lists and is recommended for most titles from other languages. Examples: The house of Rothschild: The world’s banker, 1849-1999.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline-style capitalization: core principles (rules 1–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline-style capitalization: (1) Capitalize first and last words and all major words; (2) lowercase articles (the, a, an); (3) lowercase prepositions regardless of length except when adverbial/adjectival or part of a Latin expression used adjectivally/adverbially; (4) lowercase coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor); (5) lowercase 'to' as preposition and part of an infinitive; (6) lowercase parts of proper names that would be lowercased in text (de, von); (7) lowercase the second part of a species name even if it is the last word in a title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate rules: 'Mnemonics That Work Are Better Than Rules That Do Not' (rule 1) ; 'A Little Learning Is a Dangerous Thing' (rule 2) ; species example: From Homo erectus to Homo sapiens: A Brief History (rule 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenated compounds in headline-style titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for hyphenated terms in headline-style titles: (1) Always capitalize the first element; (2) capitalize subsequent elements unless they are articles, prepositions, coordinating conjunctions, or certain modifiers; (3) if the first element is a nonstandalone prefix, do not capitalize the second element unless it is a proper noun/adjective; (4) capitalize the second element in hyphenated spelled-out numbers or simple fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Under-the-Counter Transactions (capitalize first element and following elements per rules); Cross-Stitching for Beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles containing quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a direct quotation of a sentence or independent clause is used as a title, headline-style capitalization may be imposed even for longer quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'We All Live More like Brutes Than like Humans': Labor and Capital in the Gold Rush.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics vs quotation marks for titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of italics or quotation marks depends on the type of work: titles of books and periodicals are italicized; titles of articles, chapters, and other shorter works are set in roman and enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related sections for poems, plays, movies, television, podcasts, video games, websites, musical works, works of art, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtitle capitalization and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtitle always begins with a capital letter; when referred to it is separated from the title by a colon. If an em dash is used instead of a colon, what follows is not normally considered a subtitle and need not be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Manuals of Style: Guidelines, Not Strangleholds' (headline style); 'Tapetum character states: Analytical keys' (sentence style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible editorial changes to titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to a title, preserve its original spelling and hyphenation; capitalization may be changed to headline or sentence style; an ampersand may be changed to 'and'; commas omitted for aesthetic reasons on title pages should be added when referencing the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a title page distinguishes title and subtitle only by typography, add a colon when referring to the full title. Dashes in originals should be retained; semicolons between title and subtitle may usually be changed to a colon. For older titles or multiple subtitles see detailed sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles' grammatical relation to surrounding text
rubrics_metrics.description: A title is considered a singular noun and takes a singular verb; punctuation that is part of a title should not affect the punctuation of the surrounding text (except that a sentence-ending period is omitted after a title ending in ? or !).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Waves is not a typical novel. (singular verb despite plural in title). Three stories were 'Are You a Doctor?,' 'The Library of Babel,' and 'The Diamond as Big as the Ritz.' (retain comma after first title despite question mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double titles connected by 'or' formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: For double titles connected by 'or', prefer the punctuation on the title page or head of the original; if not available, prefer a simpler punctuation form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example preference: The Tempest, or The Enchanted Island; but retain original punctuation if accessible (Moby-Dick; or, The Whale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of book and periodical titles in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles and subtitles of books and periodicals mentioned in text, notes, or bibliography are italicized and capitalized headline-style (though some publications require sentence style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full book title in notes/bibliography may be shortened in running text; initial articles (a/an/the) may be dropped if they do not fit the surrounding syntax but retain when indispensable.
